People placed lights inside root vegetable lanterns to scare away wandering spirits.

package.script: Before you carve your pumpkin, you should know why the first jack-o'-lanterns were turnips. Here's how Halloween's famous decoration swapped vegetables. Long ago in Ireland, people carved faces into big turnips and potatoes. Scotland used turnips too, and in England, large beets. They put a light inside and set them by windows and doors, to scare away wandering spirits. Picture a small, wrinkly turnip face glowing at you. Way creepier than a pumpkin. The name comes from an Irish folktale about a trickster called Stingy Jack. His ghostly light was Jack of the Lantern, later shortened to jack-o'-lantern. Then families from Ireland, Scotland and England moved to America. There they found pumpkins, which are native to the Americas. Bigger, hollow, and way easier to carve than a rock-hard turnip. So your jack-o'-lantern is a pumpkin because it was an upgrade. Would you dare carve a turnip this year? Either way, here's the one thing to remember this October.

package.title: Why Golf Balls Have 300+ Dimples
package.description:
Why do golf balls have dimples, and how many dimples on a golf ball are there? Most have 300 to 500 golf ball dimples, and they cut drag and add lift so the ball flies about twice as far as a smooth one.

In this Short: how a smooth ball drags, what the dimples do to the air, and why beat-up balls flew farther.

Sources:

scenes.text: Can you do these three body tricks? Lots of people fail at least one, and there's a real reason why. Try each one right now.
scenes.label: Can you do them?
scenes.image_prompt: First-person POV of someone looking at their own open hands resting on a clean wooden table, cinematic lighting, vertical framing

scenes.text: Trick one. Hand flat on a table, middle finger folded under. Now lift just your ring finger.
scenes.label: Lift your ring finger
scenes.image_prompt: Extreme close-up of a human hand flat on a wooden desk with middle finger tucked under palm, trying to lift ring finger, vertical framing

scenes.text: Stuck? Little tendon bridges tie it to its neighbors, so it can't lift alone.
scenes.label: Tendon bridges
scenes.image_prompt: Anatomical visualization of human hand tendons connecting the ring finger to adjacent fingers, glowing fiber lines, dark background, vertical framing

scenes.text: Trick two. Circle your right foot clockwise. Keep going, and draw a six in the air with your right hand.
scenes.label: Foot clockwise, draw a 6
scenes.image_prompt: Person sitting on a chair circling their right foot in the air while drawing the number 6 with their right index finger, split action focus, vertical framing

scenes.text: Did your foot flip? For lots of people, it does. Scientists aren't sure why, but one idea is your brain links plans for limbs on the same side.
scenes.label: Same-side brain link
scenes.image_prompt: Stylized glowing brain illustration showing neural signals firing down to the right side of the body, high-tech science aesthetic, vertical framing

scenes.text: Trick three. Roll your tongue into a U. Roughly sixty-five to eighty-one percent of people can.
scenes.label: Roll your tongue
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up portrait of a cheerful person effortlessly rolling their tongue into a U-tube shape, bright natural lighting, vertical framing

scenes.text: Textbooks called it a simple gene, but identical twins don't always match.
scenes.label: Not just simple genetics
scenes.image_prompt: Side-by-side shot of identical twins where one successfully rolls their tongue and the other tries and smiles, bright studio lighting, vertical framing

scenes.text: So now you know why your finger sticks, your foot flips, and your tongue might not roll. Which trick beat you? Tell me in the comments. Now ask a friend the same thing.
scenes.label: Which trick beat you?
scenes.image_prompt: Two friends sitting across a table laughing while testing funny hand and foot tricks together, cozy modern cafe setting, vertical framing

key_facts: The ring finger cannot easily lift independently when the middle finger is bent due to connecting fibrous tendon bands (juncturae tendinum).
Circling the right foot clockwise while drawing a number six with the right hand often causes the foot to involuntarily reverse direction due to ipsilateral motor coordination in the brain.
Between 65% and 81% of people can roll their tongue into a U shape.
Tongue rolling is not governed by a single dominant gene, as evidenced by identical twins who do not always share the trait.
